case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the government may treat a returning lawful permanent resident as an applicant for admission based on proof (including evidence developed after entry/parole) that the resident committed an offense listed in INA § 212(a)(2), or whether the government must prove—at the time of the border encounter and with conviction-level proof—that the § 101(a)(13)(C) exception applies.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) (returning LPRs treated as seeking admission if they have 'committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2)'); 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2) (criminal grounds of inadmissibility); related removal/admission framework including 8 U.S.C. §§ 1227 (deportability) and 1229a (removal proceedings/burdens) and the referenced INA § 212(h) waiver.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Attorney General argues that Congress adopted a conduct-based admission framework for returning LPRs: if the person has 'committed' a § 212(a)(2) offense, DHS may treat the person as seeking admission. That framework would be undermined if DHS had to establish conviction-level proof at the border or could rely only on what was known at the moment of inspection. The government contends it can satisfy the applicable burden in subsequent § 1229a proceedings using later-developed evidence (including a later conviction or disposition) to show the person committed the offense and therefore fell within § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5), supporting removability on inadmissibility grounds and defeating eligibility for relief such as a § 212(h) waiver where inapplicable.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Lau argues the Second Circuit correctly rejected the government’s approach: the government cannot retroactively convert a returning LPR into an arriving applicant for admission based on post-entry developments, and must prove the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception under the proper standard during removal proceedings. He also argues the government forfeited any challenge to the clear-and-convincing evidence burden by accepting BIA precedent below. Separately, he contends the issue is not outcome-determinative because removability ultimately turns on whether his trademark-counterfeiting offense qualifies as a crime involving moral turpitude under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) (and related CIMT analysis), which the petition does not ask the Court to decide, making the case a poor vehicle.
key_precedents: Doe v. Attorney General, 659 F.3d 266 (3d Cir. 2011) (referenced regarding supplying a burden standard under federal common law for § 1101(a)(13)(C) exceptions)
BIA precedent (unnamed in the excerpts) indicating the default standard for stripping LPR protections / proving § 1101(a)(13)(C) exceptions is clear and convincing evidence

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press a serious fairness/reliance concern—whether DHS may “retroactively” treat an LPR as seeking admission based on later-developed evidence—but that argument ultimately asks us to add a timing/knowledge constraint to § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) that Congress did not write. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, the trigger is conduct-based (“has committed”), and the post-IIRIRA structure channels the evidentiary testing and burden allocation into § 1229a rather than forcing a merits adjudication at primary inspection. Vartelas matters here chiefly as it cautions against reintroducing Fleuti-like, extra-textual insulation once Congress replaced it with enumerated exceptions; the fairness concerns are better handled through the procedures and burdens in removal court than by freezing the government to what it could prove at the border. A minimalist disposition remains appropriate: later-developed evidence may be considered in § 1229a to establish the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) threshold, reserving broader questions about burdens, due process limits, and the ultimate inadmissibility determination for a cleaner case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness-and-reliance objection does not overcome the statutory text: § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) asks whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense, a conduct-based criterion that contains no contemporaneous-knowledge or inspection-stage timing limitation, and we are not at liberty to add one. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, IIRIRA’s structure channels contested factfinding into § 1229a removal proceedings, making it entirely consistent to consider later-developed evidence there rather than forcing a border-time merits adjudication. Vartelas, as Roberts notes, describes Congress’s narrowing of Fleuti through enumerated exceptions, which counsels against recreating Fleuti-like protections by judicially grafting an atextual “freeze” on the Government’s proof. Any due process concerns are handled by the burdens and procedures Congress prescribed in § 1229a, not by rewriting the trigger in § 1101(a)(13)(C).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance/fairness objection is serious, but it cannot overcome the statutory text Congress chose: § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) asks whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—an objective, conduct-based criterion with no temporal or government-knowledge limitation. As the Chief Justice stresses, the post-IIRIRA structure contemplates that inspection decisions may be provisional and that the definitive factfinding (with burdens and procedural protections) occurs in § 1229a proceedings, so considering later-developed evidence is not a retroactive “end run” but the mechanism Congress designed. Vartelas, which Roberts and Kagan invoke, underscores that IIRIRA narrowed Fleuti through enumerated exceptions; importing an atextual “provable-at-the-border” rule would effectively recreate Fleuti-like insulation for returning LPRs. Any arbitrariness concerns are better policed through due-process limits and the Government’s burden in removal court, not by rewriting the trigger to freeze the evidentiary record at primary inspection.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that “has committed” is conduct-based and that § 1229a is the ordinary forum for testing evidence, but that does not resolve the distinct structural question of when the Government may strip a returning LPR of the presumption against being treated as “seeking admission” in the first place. Vartelas matters here not because it restores Fleuti wholesale, but because it recognizes the special reliance and settled-expectations interests of returning LPRs—interests that are undermined if DHS can admit/parole at the border and later, based on evidence developed only afterward, retroactively recast the person as an arriving applicant and trigger harsher procedural consequences. Justice Alito’s workability/public-safety concern is real, yet it is met by straightforward deportability proceedings under § 1227 with full § 1229a protections; expanding § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) into an after-the-fact lever is an unnecessary and inequitable way to manage risk. Under a pragmatic, fairness-centered approach attentive to real-world process effects, I remain persuaded the exception should be applied in a clear, timely, administrable manner tethered to the border encounter rather than later-developed proof.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the fairness/reliance worry that DHS can effectively “retroactively” convert an admitted/paroled LPR into an arriving applicant, but the text she must overcome is Congress’s conduct-based trigger—an LPR is seeking admission if he “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—without any contemporaneous-knowledge or moment-of-inspection limitation. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, IIRIRA’s structure channels the real evidentiary testing into § 1229a, and freezing the government to what it could prove at primary inspection would be an atextual rule that also misfits Congress’s sequencing of screening first, adjudication later. Vartelas (as Roberts and Barrett note) confirms Congress narrowed Fleuti via enumerated exceptions; importing a timing constraint would functionally recreate Fleuti-like insulation rather than apply the exception Congress wrote. The respondent’s arbitrariness concern is better addressed by insisting on proper burdens and procedural protections in removal court, not by rewriting § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) to bar later-developed evidence.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness and reliance concerns are serious, but they ask us to add a timing/knowledge limitation Congress did not write into § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5): the text turns on whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense, not whether DHS could prove it at primary inspection. As Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice emphasize, IIRIRA’s structure channels adjudicative factfinding into § 1229a, making it an awkward fit to freeze the evidentiary record at the border and effectively recreate a Fleuti-like protection by judicial implication. Vartelas, which the Chief and Justice Kagan discuss, underscores that Congress replaced Fleuti with enumerated exceptions; reading those exceptions to permit later-developed proof in removal proceedings respects that choice while leaving due process to be policed through burdens and procedures in § 1229a rather than statutory revision. I therefore remain with petitioner and would favor a narrow holding limited to the permissibility of considering later-developed evidence to establish the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) trigger.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness/reliance point remains the respondent’s strongest argument, but I do not see a textual or structural basis to freeze § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) at the moment of inspection when Congress used the objective, conduct-based phrase “has committed,” not a knowledge- or timing-based formulation. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, IIRIRA’s design channels the ultimate factfinding—under procedural protections and burdens—into § 1229a, and importing a contemporaneous-proof requirement would effectively recreate a Fleuti-like insulation Congress narrowed (as Vartelas describes) while creating serious workability problems at ports of entry. Justice Jackson’s concern about “after-the-fact reclassification” is mitigated because the statute itself makes “seeking admission” turn on the underlying conduct, and any arbitrariness is best policed through due process and burden-of-proof rules in removal court rather than by rewriting the statutory trigger. I therefore stay with petitioner on the narrow ground that later-developed evidence may be considered in § 1229a to establish the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) condition, leaving harder due-process edge cases for another day.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the fairness/reliance concern that after-the-fact proof can "retroactively" convert a returning LPR into an arriving applicant with harsher procedural consequences, but that argument depends on reading a timing/knowledge limitation into § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) that the text does not supply. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress wrote a conduct-based trigger—whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—and, after IIRIRA, located the central factfinding and burden-allocation in § 1229a proceedings, which are designed to test evidence (including evidence developed after inspection) with procedural safeguards. Vartelas’s account of IIRIRA’s partial abrogation of Fleuti cuts against using fairness concerns to recreate, through interpretation, an extra-textual insulation for returning LPRs that Congress narrowed by enumerating specific exceptions. Any inequity from delayed proof is better addressed through due process and the Government’s burden in removal court, not by freezing the evidentiary record at the port of entry.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that “has committed” in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) is conduct-based and, in the abstract, can be litigated in § 1229a proceedings. But that textual point does not resolve the threshold structural problem: § 1101(a)(13)(C) is the narrow gateway that authorizes treating a returning LPR as “seeking admission,” with immediate, status-altering procedural consequences, and I remain unpersuaded that Congress meant that gateway to swing open based on after-the-fact evidence once the Government has already processed the person as inside the country. Vartelas’s account of IIRIRA narrowing Fleuti cautions against judicially expanding protections, but it also underscores Congress’s decision to enumerate specific circumstances for stripping the returning-LPR default—supporting a tether to the border encounter rather than a retroactive reclassification rule. As Justice Sotomayor emphasizes, the Government’s legitimate enforcement interests can be pursued through § 1227 removability with full § 1229a process, which mitigates the fairness and reliance harms that flow from post hoc “arriving alien” treatment.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text Congress enacted in IIRIRA treats a returning LPR as seeking admission if he “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5), and nothing in that language confines proof to what was known at the moment of inspection or demands conviction-level evidence as a prerequisite to applying the exception in later § 1229a removal proceedings. Reading the statute to allow the Government to establish the § 1101(a)(13)(C) trigger in the ensuing adjudication—subject to the ordinary procedural protections and burdens in removal court—better fits Congress’s 1996 choice to replace Fleuti’s judge-made insulation of brief trips with a defined set of exceptions restoring “meaningful border scrutiny.” See Rosenberg v. Fleuti, 374 U.S. 449 (1963); see also Vartelas v. Holder, 566 U.S. 257, 260–61 (2012) (describing § 1101(a)(13)(C) as partially codifying/abrogating Fleuti). A narrow holding recognizing that later-developed evidence may be considered to prove commission under § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5)—while leaving untouched the separate CIMT/§ 1182(a)(2) merits question and any settled clear-and-convincing standard the agency applies—best preserves institutional legitimacy and adheres to the statutory framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” which is conduct-based language and does not require that the offense be established with conviction-level proof at the moment of inspection. Nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C) limits the government to evidence available at the border encounter; under the ordinary removal framework, DHS may prove in subsequent § 1229a proceedings—using later-developed evidence—that the alien falls within the statutory exception and therefore is properly treated as seeking admission. Congress enacted § 1101(a)(13)(C) in 1996 to supplant Fleuti’s judge-made “innocent, casual, and brief” limitation and to restore meaningful scrutiny of returning LPRs with disqualifying criminal conduct, and courts should not reintroduce a timing/knowledge restriction the statute does not contain. To the extent any prior understandings would bar later-developed proof, they must yield to the statute’s original public meaning and Congress’s chosen words in IIRIRA.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) turns on whether the returning LPR has “committed” an offense identified in § 1182(a)(2), and Congress’s choice of “committed” (rather than “convicted”) supports a conduct-based inquiry that can be proven in later § 1229a removal proceedings, including with evidence developed after parole. Reading the statute to require conviction-level proof at the moment of inspection would collapse Congress’s screening-and-adjudication structure at the border and undermine the practical risk-management tool of parole, contrary to IIRIRA’s evident purpose to restore meaningful scrutiny after Fleuti. The respondent’s contemporaneous-facts limitation has no clear textual anchor in § 1101(a)(13)(C) and would create serious public-safety consequences by forcing admission when the government cannot yet assemble proof at the border. Congress’s 1996 replacement of the Fleuti “entry” doctrine with the detailed “admission” framework in § 1101(a)(13)(C) indicates that the government may establish the exception in subsequent proceedings rather than being confined to what was known at inspection.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: INA § 101(a)(13)(C) sets out narrow, threshold exceptions for when a returning LPR may be treated as “seeking admission,” and the government should not be permitted to retroactively strip that status based on evidence developed only after DHS has already allowed entry or parole. Congress’s post-IIRIRA framework partially codified and partially abrogated Rosenberg v. Fleuti, but it still reflects a judgment that LPRs retain significant protections at the border absent a properly established § 101(a)(13)(C) exception, and fairness demands a clear showing before converting an LPR into an arriving applicant. Allowing post hoc proof to trigger § 101(a)(13)(C)(5) would expand government power in a way that risks arbitrary outcomes and undermines reliance interests and access to justice for long-term residents, while the government remains able to pursue removal under the deportability grounds in 8 U.S.C. § 1227 when appropriate. Given the severe consequences of treating an LPR as inadmissible, the better reading is that DHS must establish the applicability of § 101(a)(13)(C) at the inspection/charging stage under the heightened protections traditionally attached to stripping LPR status.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of INA § 101(a)(13)(C)(5), 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5), turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed” an offense identified in § 212(a)(2), not on what DHS could prove at the moment of inspection; Congress’s choice of the conduct-based verb suggests the inquiry may be adjudicated (with ordinary evidentiary development) in the ensuing § 1229a removal proceedings. Requiring conviction-level proof at the border or freezing the record at the time of encounter would undercut IIRIRA’s replacement of Fleuti’s judge-made limits with a more administrable, purposefully stricter admission framework, as recognized in Vartelas’s description of § 101(a)(13)(C) as partially abrogating Fleuti. Workability also favors the government’s position: § 1229a already supplies a structured forum for factfinding and burdens, and nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C) imposes a timing restriction that would bar later-developed evidence from showing the LPR fell within the exception. Finally, while the ultimate inadmissibility ground may depend on the CIMT question under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I), that merits/vehicle concern does not justify reading an extra-textual timing limitation into § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of INA § 101(a)(13)(C)(5), 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5), asks whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” a conduct-based inquiry that does not by its terms freeze the government to only what was known at primary inspection or require conviction-level proof at the border. Congress in IIRIRA replaced “entry” with “admission” and limited Fleuti’s judge-made insulation for brief trips abroad; that reform is best read to restore meaningful border scrutiny for LPRs who fall within the enumerated exceptions, rather than to create a timing rule that would bar later-developed proof in § 1229a proceedings. In removal proceedings, the government may establish the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception using admissible, later-developed evidence consistent with the statutory framework for adjudication and burdens under 8 U.S.C. § 1229a, and nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C) requires the government to decide the “seeking admission” question irrevocably at the moment of encounter. While due process and any applicable burden of proof remain constraints, the statute’s plain terms and IIRIRA’s abrogation of Fleuti’s broader shield foreclose the respondent’s proposed temporal and “conviction-at-the-border” limitations.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of INA § 101(a)(13)(C)(5), 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5), turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed” an offense identified in § 212(a)(2), which is naturally read as a conduct-based trigger rather than a requirement that DHS possess conviction-level proof at the moment of inspection. IIRIRA was enacted to narrow the Fleuti regime and restore meaningful border scrutiny of returning LPRs with criminal conduct, and that history supports allowing the Government to establish the § 101(a)(13)(C) exception in § 1229a proceedings using later-developed evidence. Requiring DHS to prove the exception at the border based only on then-known facts would be impractical and would undermine the statutory scheme that places the ultimate burden and factfinding in removal proceedings. Because Congress used “committed” (not “convicted”) in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5), the Government may treat the LPR as seeking admission upon proving, in subsequent proceedings, that the offense was committed within the meaning of § 1182(a)(2).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of INA § 101(a)(13)(C)(5), 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5), turns on whether a returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” which is naturally read as a conduct-based criterion and does not specify that the Government must possess conviction-level proof at the moment of inspection or be limited to evidence known at the border. In the integrated removal scheme Congress enacted in IIRIRA—particularly § 1229a’s adjudicatory forum and burdens—the Government may prove the applicability of § 1101(a)(13)(C) in subsequent proceedings using competent evidence, including later-developed evidence, rather than converting the border encounter into a merits trial. This reading also coheres with Congress’s IIRIRA response to Rosenberg v. Fleuti, 374 U.S. 449 (1963), which narrowed the circumstances in which returning LPRs avoid being treated as seeking admission, and it preserves the practical role of parole and inspection without silently imposing a temporal/evidentiary restriction absent from the statutory text. Precedent about burdens (including BIA practice applying a clear-and-convincing standard to § 1101(a)(13)(C) exceptions) addresses the level of proof in § 1229a proceedings, not atextual requirements that proof be fixed at the border or limited to convictions.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: INA § 101(a)(13)(C) sets out narrow, status-altering exceptions under which a returning LPR is treated as “seeking admission,” and treating that threshold as satisfied by post-entry, later-developed proof risks collapsing the statutory line Congress drew between admission screening and in-country removal, with significant procedural consequences under § 1229a and the burdens that attach. The government’s conduct-based reading of “has committed” in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) should not be construed to authorize retroactive conversion of an admitted/paroled LPR into an arriving applicant without the government meeting a clear, fair, and administrable showing tethered to the border encounter, especially given the historically weighty due-process interests LPRs possess when returning from travel. Congress’s 1996 response to Rosenberg v. Fleuti limited LPR immunity from inspection, but it did so by enumerating specific exceptions—not by authorizing after-the-fact reclassification untethered from the inspection decision. Consistent with procedural fairness principles reflected in BIA practice and the structure of §§ 1227 and 1229a, the government must prove the § 101(a)(13)(C) exception in removal proceedings under a demanding standard, rather than relying on later-developed evidence to justify the initial arriving-alien treatment.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether DHS may treat a returning lawful permanent resident as an applicant for admission under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) based on proof (including evidence obtained after the person is paroled into the United States) that the LPR committed a § 1182(a)(2) offense before reentry, or whether removability must instead be pursued only under the deportability grounds in § 1227 (and/or only with conviction-level proof at the time of entry).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C) (when an LPR is regarded as seeking admission), especially § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) (LPR who has committed an offense identified in § 1182(a)(2)); 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2) (criminal grounds of inadmissibility, including crimes involving moral turpitude); 8 U.S.C. § 1227 (grounds of deportability); plus related burden/standard-of-proof provisions in removal proceedings (generally 8 U.S.C. § 1229a).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Attorney General argues that Congress created a conduct-based admission framework for returning LPRs: if an LPR has "committed" a § 1182(a)(2) offense before return, the LPR fits § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) and can be placed in inadmissibility-based removal proceedings. DHS should be able to rely on evidence establishing the pre-entry commission of the offense even if the evidence (or conviction) becomes available only after the person is paroled in for deferred inspection; requiring conviction-level proof at the border would undermine border integrity and public safety and would be inconsistent with the statutory term "committed."
case_analysis.respondent_position: Lau argues the Second Circuit correctly limited the government’s ability to treat returning LPRs as applicants for admission: the government must prove the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception under the applicable burden and cannot bootstrap inadmissibility by relying on post-entry developments to retroactively classify the person as seeking admission at the time of reentry. He also contends the government forfeited any challenge to the standard of proof by accepting the clear-and-convincing standard below; and, in any event, the case is a poor vehicle because the outcome ultimately turns on whether his offense qualifies as a crime involving moral turpitude (CIMT), an issue not presented for Supreme Court review.
key_precedents: Doe v. Attorney General, 659 F.3d 266 (3d Cir. 2011) (burden/standard issue for proving a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception, referenced in the briefing as part of a developing split/approach)

Board of Immigration Appeals precedent (unnamed in the excerpts) treating the default standard for stripping LPR protections as "clear and convincing evidence" and allocating the burden to the government to prove a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson raise the most serious point: that allowing post-parole proof to trigger § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) can look like after-the-fact relabeling with real detention and procedural consequences. But the statutory trigger is framed as a historical fact—whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—and, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, § 1229a is the adjudicatory forum Congress provided for proving such past conduct with specified burdens; nothing in the text supplies an evidence-at-entry cutoff. Vartelas, which Justice Jackson invokes, underscores the gravity of treating an LPR as seeking admission, but it does not rewrite “committed” into “convicted (or provable) at the booth,” and we can preserve institutional legitimacy through a narrow holding limited to the timing/proof question while leaving open the underlying scope of “committed” and any distinct due process challenges to particular parole/detention practices. Under a minimalist, precedent-respecting approach, importing an atextual timing rule would recreate a Fleuti-like insulation IIRIRA replaced with enumerated exceptions, whereas requiring the Government to prove pre-entry commission in § 1229a proceedings adequately addresses the fairness concern without altering the statute’s design.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson emphasize fairness and the entry-time consequences of being deemed an arriving alien, but that concern cannot justify inserting a time-of-entry evidentiary cutoff that the text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) does not contain. The statute asks whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—a backward-looking, conduct-based fact—so, as the Chief Justice notes, the relevant question is what happened before reentry, not what DHS could prove at the inspection booth. Vartelas does not change the analysis: it recognizes IIRIRA’s enumerated exceptions and its comments about convictions/admissions as common proof do not rewrite “committed” into “convicted (or provable) at entry,” as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan explain. Structural and procedural concerns are addressed by § 1229a’s adjudicatory process and the Government’s burden there, not by atextual limits that effectively restore Fleuti-like insulation Congress displaced.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness/structure objection about “after-the-fact relabeling” is the best point for Respondent, but it asks us to graft an atextual, time-of-entry evidentiary cutoff onto § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) that Congress did not enact. As the Chief emphasizes, the statutory trigger is whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—a historical, conduct-based fact—while § 1229a supplies the adjudicatory mechanism and burdens for proving that fact, often with later-developed evidence. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Vartelas does not undermine that reading; Vartelas’s discussion of convictions/admissions describes common proof and reliance interests, not a rule that “committed” means “provable at the booth,” and importing such a limitation would recreate the kind of Fleuti-like insulation IIRIRA replaced with enumerated exceptions. The practical consequences Sotomayor identifies are real, but under a textualist approach they are addressed by insisting the Government carry its burden in removal proceedings, not by rewriting the statute’s operative verb.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that “has committed” in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) is backward-looking and can be proved in § 1229a with later-developed evidence, but that does not answer the distinct structural question of when DHS may classify a returning LPR as “seeking an admission” in the first place. My concern is that, once DHS has exercised discretion to parole the LPR into the country, allowing it later to relabel the person as an arriving alien based on newly assembled proof collapses Congress’s careful division between inadmissibility (§ 1182) and deportability (§ 1227) and magnifies detention and process consequences for settled residents without clear notice at the border. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Vartelas does not undermine this: Vartelas’s emphasis on reliance/fairness and its observation that clause (v) “appears to avert to” convictions/admissions supports requiring an administrable entry-time threshold for invoking the (C) exceptions, rather than a roving, post hoc status switch. The government retains ample authority to proceed under § 1227 after parole/admission, so an entry-focused reading better fits the statute’s operation and the real-world stakes for vulnerable lawful permanent residents.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press a serious structural/fairness concern: that parole and later-developed evidence could let DHS “retroactively” reclassify an LPR as an arriving alien and thereby manipulate the inadmissibility/deportability tracks. But on my textualist premises, § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on a backward-looking historical fact—whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—not on what DHS could prove at the inspection booth, and § 1229a is the ordinary mechanism Congress supplied for proving such past facts with allocated burdens. As Justice Barrett notes, Vartelas’s observation about convictions/admissions is descriptive of common proof, not a clear statutory command that the proof must predate reentry; importing an evidence-at-entry cutoff would effectively rewrite “committed” into “provably committed at entry,” reintroducing a Fleuti-like insulation Congress narrowed in IIRIRA. The fair-notice and workability worries are better met—consistent with the Chief’s approach—by insisting DHS carry its burden in removal proceedings and by keeping the holding narrow on timing/proof, rather than adding a temporal limitation the statute does not contain.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press a serious structural/fairness concern: that permitting post-parole proof “retroactively” converts an LPR into an arriving alien and blurs the §§ 1182/1227 divide. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) is written in backward-looking, conduct-based terms—whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—and nothing in the enacted text adds a time-of-entry evidentiary cutoff; importing one would effectively amend “committed” to “provable at the booth.” Vartelas, which Justice Jackson invokes, underscores the consequences of admission treatment but does not rewrite the statutory trigger into a conviction-at-entry requirement; instead, § 1229a supplies the forum where DHS must prove the pre-entry commission under the applicable burdens, which is the procedural protection Congress chose. Because the respondents’ proposed timing rule lacks a textual anchor and would reintroduce a Fleuti-like insulation Congress displaced with enumerated exceptions, I remain with Petitioner.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor raise the hardest point: that allowing post-parole evidence to establish clause (v) risks an after-the-fact shift to the inadmissibility/arriving-alien track with serious detention and procedural consequences. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) is written in conduct terms (“has committed”), and nothing in the statutory text makes the applicability of that exception depend on what DHS could prove at the inspection booth; § 1229a is the forum Congress provided to litigate historical facts with the government bearing the burden. Vartelas, which Justice Jackson invokes, underscores the gravity of treating an LPR as seeking admission, yet it does not supply a textual basis to rewrite “committed” into a conviction-at-entry or evidence-at-entry rule, and adopting such a cutoff would reintroduce a Fleuti-like insulation Congress narrowed through IIRIRA’s enumerated exceptions. The proper safeguard, consistent with administrability and precedent, is a narrow holding that DHS may rely on later-developed evidence in removal proceedings to prove pre-entry commission, while requiring the government to satisfy the applicable burdens and procedures there.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s structural/fairness objection—that DHS can parole an LPR and later “retroactively” relabel the person an arriving alien—highlights real practical consequences, but it cannot justify adding a time-of-entry evidentiary cutoff Congress did not write. As the Chief and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) uses conduct-based language (“has committed”), which asks a historical question; importing an “evidence available at the booth” requirement would effectively amend the text to “has been convicted (or provably committed at entry).” Justice Jackson’s reliance on Vartelas underscores the gravity of treating LPRs as seeking admission, but Vartelas’s observation about convictions/admissions as common proof does not override Congress’s choice of “committed,” and § 1229a supplies the adjudicatory forum and burdens that address the fairness concern without rewriting the statute. I therefore remain with the Petitioner on the narrow point that later-developed evidence may be used in removal proceedings to establish pre-entry commission of a § 1182(a)(2) offense.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the best textual point: § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) is conduct-based (“has committed”) and does not expressly limit DHS to evidence available at the inspection booth, and § 1229a is the ordinary forum for proving historical facts. But that reading undervalues how § 1101(a)(13)(C) operates as an entry-time classification rule that triggers immediate, concrete consequences (detention posture, burden framing, and the inadmissibility/deportability divide) and should not be susceptible to after-the-fact relabeling once DHS has chosen parole/deferred inspection. Vartelas’s emphasis on the gravity of treating an LPR as seeking admission strengthens my view that we should adopt an administrable, procedurally fair rule keyed to the government’s choice and showing at reentry, while leaving DHS fully able to proceed under § 1227 after entry if later-developed evidence supports removability. Under my pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, the government’s later ability to prove commission in § 1229a does not cure the destabilizing structural and reliance harms of permitting retroactive “arriving alien” treatment based on post-parole proof.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) makes the default rule that a returning LPR is not seeking admission, but it expressly withdraws that protection where the government proves the LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v)—language Congress adopted in IIRIRA to curtail Fleuti’s insulation of returning residents from meaningful border scrutiny. Nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) ties the inquiry to the evidence available at the port of entry or precludes DHS from relying on proof developed during deferred inspection after parole, so long as the agency proves the pre-entry commission of the § 1182(a)(2) offense in removal proceedings under § 1229a. A contrary, timing-based limitation risks reintroducing the very “innocent, casual, and brief excursion” loophole Congress narrowed in 1996, and it would force DHS to proceed only under § 1227 even when Congress specified inadmissibility treatment for returning LPRs who have committed § 1182(a)(2) offenses. The holding can remain narrow: DHS may treat the LPR as an applicant for admission under § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) upon proving pre-return commission of a § 1182(a)(2) offense, without resolving any separate CIMT-classification question.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C) makes the default rule that an LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission” unless one of six enumerated exceptions applies; subsection (v) turns on whether the LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” which is conduct-based and not limited to conviction-level proof or evidence available at the instant of inspection. Nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) or the parole provisions forbids DHS from relying on later-obtained proof to establish that the pre-reentry conduct occurred, so long as the Government carries its burden in removal proceedings under § 1229a. Congress enacted IIRIRA in 1996 to replace the judicial Fleuti regime with this specific statutory framework, restoring meaningful border scrutiny for returning LPRs who engaged in criminal conduct, and we should adhere to that enacted text rather than impose extra-statutory temporal or evidentiary limitations. Rosenberg v. Fleuti is therefore not controlling after IIRIRA’s redefinition of “admission” and its express exceptions, and any contrary limitation would improperly rewrite the statute.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) sets the exclusive conditions under which a returning LPR is “regarded as seeking an admission,” and subsection (v) turns on whether the alien “has committed” an offense identified in § 1182(a)(2), a conduct-based term that does not require a conviction at the moment of inspection. Nothing in the text limits DHS to evidence available at the border; in removal proceedings under § 1229a the government may prove the predicate facts (subject to the applicable burden) and practical administration would be severely impaired if DHS had to forgo § 1182 inadmissibility whenever proof crystallizes after parole for deferred inspection. Reading the statute to force the government into § 1227 deportability grounds would improperly narrow Congress’s 1996 IIRIRA replacement of Fleuti’s judge-made insulation and would undermine the border-screening function Congress sought to restore. This interpretation is consistent with IIRIRA’s partial abrogation/codification of Fleuti and the statutory structure distinguishing “admission” determinations from later-accruing deportability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) establishes a strong presumption that an LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission,” and its listed exceptions—including § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v)—are best read to require DHS to determine, at the time of reentry, whether the government can carry its burden to strip that protection; allowing DHS to use post-parole evidence to retroactively transform an admitted LPR into an “arriving alien” would evade the statute’s structure and channel removals into § 1182 rather than the deportability scheme in § 1227. That reading fits IIRIRA’s partial codification/abrogation of Fleuti: Congress limited when an LPR’s “brief excursion” triggers admission consequences, but did not authorize after-the-fact relabeling once DHS has chosen to parole the person into the United States for deferred inspection. The government still retains ample authority to proceed under § 1227 after admission, and requiring proof sufficient at entry (at least under the government’s accepted clear-and-convincing standard for § 1101(a)(13)(C) exceptions) better protects settled LPRs and avoids unfair surprise and prolonged detention based on later-developed allegations of “committed” conduct. This approach also accords with the statute’s temporal cues (present-tense, entry-focused exceptions) and with the fairness and reliance interests recognized in Vartelas’s discussion of Fleuti’s legacy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed” an offense identified in § 1182(a)(2), and that conduct-focused phrasing is naturally read to permit DHS to prove the pre-reentry commission of the offense in later § 1229a proceedings, including with evidence obtained after parole for deferred inspection. Reading the statute to require conviction-level proof at the port of entry would effectively rewrite “committed” into “convicted” and would undermine Congress’s 1996 IIRIRA choice to cabin Fleuti and restore meaningful border scrutiny for certain returning LPRs. That said, the government must still carry the burden (typically by clear and convincing evidence) to establish the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception in removal proceedings, which preserves workability and protects settled LPR expectations without nullifying clause (v). This interpretation aligns with Vartelas’s account that IIRIRA partially abrogated Fleuti by specifying when LPRs are treated as seeking admission and does so in a way that makes the statutory scheme coherent across §§ 1101(a)(13), 1182, and 1229a.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C) makes the default rule that an LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission,” but it then creates enumerated exceptions—including when the LPR “has committed” an offense identified in § 1182(a)(2), § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v). Read in ordinary terms, “has committed” turns on past conduct, not on what evidence the government happened to possess at the inspection booth; nothing in the statute limits DHS to conviction-level proof at the moment of reentry or forbids reliance on evidence obtained after parole/deferral to establish the pre-entry commission of the offense. Congress enacted § 1101(a)(13)(C) in IIRIRA to displace the more lenient Fleuti-era regime and restore meaningful border scrutiny for returning LPRs with criminal conduct, and that purpose aligns with the conduct-based phrasing Congress chose. Provided the government carries the burden assigned in removal proceedings (see 8 U.S.C. § 1229a) to prove the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) exception, the statute permits treating the returning LPR as an applicant for admission rather than forcing the government into § 1227 deportability grounds alone.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) creates a presumption that a returning LPR is not seeking admission, but Congress in IIRIRA specified six exceptions, including § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) for an LPR who has “committed an offense identified in § 1182(a)(2).” The text focuses on pre-entry conduct (“committed”), not on whether DHS possessed conviction-level proof at the port of entry, and reading in a temporal/evidentiary limitation would undermine the border-scrutiny regime Congress adopted to displace Fleuti’s broader insulation of returning LPRs. Consistent with BIA practice (e.g., Matter of Rivens) the government must still prove the exception in removal proceedings (typically by clear and convincing evidence), but it may rely on evidence developed after parole/inspection to establish that the offense was committed before reentry. That approach is more workable and aligned with Congress’s post-Fleuti framework preserving only a limited portion of the old doctrine while restoring meaningful inspection for LPRs with § 1182(a)(2) criminal conduct.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed” an offense “identified in” § 1182(a)(2), and “committed” is conduct-based rather than conviction-based; nothing in the statute limits the government to evidence in hand at the moment of reentry. In removal proceedings under § 1229a, the government may prove historical facts using later-obtained evidence, so long as it satisfies the applicable burden (often clear and convincing) to establish the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception. Vartelas recognizes the six exceptions and (in dicta) suggests conviction/admission is an ordinary way to show commission, but it does not rewrite “committed” to mean “convicted before entry,” nor does it impose an evidentiary time-of-entry cutoff. Accordingly, DHS may treat the LPR as an applicant for admission upon proving pre-reentry commission of a § 1182(a)(2) offense even if the proof is developed after parole, leaving any burden/vehicle disputes to be addressed on remand.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) establishes a strong presumption that returning lawful permanent residents are not “seeking admission,” and DHS must satisfy the statutory exception in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) consistent with procedural fairness and the statute’s timing logic at reentry. Allowing DHS to parole an LPR into the country and then later, based on post-entry obtained evidence, retroactively relabel the person an “applicant for admission” risks collapsing the distinct inadmissibility and deportability frameworks Congress set out in §§ 1182 and 1227, and it invites practical consequences that undermine predictable status and due process. Vartelas v. Holder underscores the significant legal consequences that flow from treating an LPR as an applicant for admission and cautions against attaching new or expanded admission disabilities to prior conduct; its observation that § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) “appears to avert to” convictions or admissions reinforces the need for a clear, administrable threshold. On this reading, DHS must proceed under § 1227 when it cannot establish at the time of entry—under the government’s burden in removal proceedings, see § 1229a—the factual predicate to strip LPR entry protections.
